principle: Make every button press visibly register the moment it happens
why: Play is a two-way flow: information goes from the player's hands to the computer and back to their eyes and ears, and the hand side is vital, so an action with no reaction feels lacking. Lag from TVs and networks can never be fully removed, but the game can still tell players right away that their input was received. Impact sounds must never feel late, because players need a reaction to their attack immediately.
how_to_apply: On the first frame after an attack input, jump to a clearly different pose instead of easing out of idle. Give every accepted press an unambiguous signal (pose, sound, highlight). In menus accept confirm from more than one button; during cutscenes let any press bring up a skip prompt. Shape hit sounds so they reach a strong level almost instantly. Count the frames from press to first visible change for every action and treat that number as a design value.
anti_pattern: Smoothly interpolating from standby into the windup, which delays the visible response; buttons that do nothing in some state; ambiguous feedback that leaves players unsure the press registered; impact sounds with a slow attack.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the pose changes drastically the instant a Smash Attack is pressed, then the fighter holds and shakes while charging. Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack comes out one frame after input. The Pong-style dial games that impressed young Sakurai moved objects directly on a bright, flashy screen.
review_question: How many frames pass between a press and the first visible or audible response, and does any press in any game state get no reaction at all?
keywords: responsiveness input feedback acknowledgement instant response press reaction dead buttons action reaction snappy controls input confirmation first frame

principle: Stop the action at every big moment: hits, boss defeats and deaths
why: Whether hit stop is present completely changes how heavy a hit feels. A boss stop (the screen stops and flashes) is vital for feeling the defeat. In many shoot 'em ups players die without realizing it; if their takeaway is 'Wait, I got hit?', the game has only told them something went wrong, a missed opportunity. Stops are relatively easy to implement and belong in every genre.
how_to_apply: Freeze attacker and target briefly when a hit lands. On a boss defeat, freeze and flash the screen before the defeat sequence. When the player takes damage or loses a life, pause for an instant so the point of impact is visible. For the biggest moments (finishing blows, boss kills) layer a full stop with screen shake, a flash and slow motion. Compare builds with and without the stop.
anti_pattern: Treating stops as minor polish; deaths the player never saw happen; stopping the screen everywhere at the same strength so big moments don't stand out.
example: Kirby's Adventure (NES) stops and flashes the screen when a boss falls and stops the action when Kirby loses a life. Fantasy Zone (1986) stops the screen for a second when you're hit; Defender (1980) builds the stop into its hit effect. Final Fight's hit stop defined its feel. Smash Ultimate's Finish Zoom extends the boss-stop idea, and finishing blows stop the screen completely.
review_question: When the player lands a hit, beats a boss or dies, does the game stop long enough for them to see exactly what happened and feel it?
keywords: hitstop hit-stop hit stop freeze frame impact pause boss stop finish zoom stop effect death pause slow motion heavy hits big moments

principle: Hunt down input lag across the whole display and audio chain
why: Even a game with great response time is ruined by display or audio delay. At E3 2018 the Smash Ultimate setup had enough lag to ruin the controls and nobody noticed until Sakurai did: many people don't recognize lag when they see it. Modern TVs and monitors do heavy image processing, and more post-processing means more lag; during a recorded session his shots kept going astray until he switched to a low-lag monitor.
how_to_apply: Before any playtest, demo, capture or event, press jump in a game that responds instantly (a 2D NES game, not a 3D one) on that exact setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press. Use Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off every picture enhancement. Check sound separately and use an analog or low-latency audio path if hit sounds arrive late. Convert latency specs to frames: 16.67 ms is one frame at 60 fps. Rule out display lag before retuning any timing.
anti_pattern: Trusting that someone else already tested the setup; judging lag with a 3D game; leaving TV post-processing on; retuning the game to compensate for a laggy screen.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate at Nintendo's E3 2018 Treehouse: Live. Special Crossover #2: Sakurai swaps to the monitor from his 'Mr. Sakurai Presents' recordings mid-session. Brawl's speed was lowered partly because frame skips stood out online the higher the input density.
review_question: Has someone checked this exact screen, capture and audio setup for lag today, using a game known to respond instantly?
keywords: input lag latency display lag delay game mode low latency mode TV post-processing audio delay frame delay 16.67 ms online lag netcode responsiveness demo setup

principle: Make attacks that look like they connect actually connect
why: In a fast game with coordinate-based movement, hitboxes mapped tightly to the sword or fist make attacks miss and players grow more and more stressed. Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or keep hitting after the swing ends, feel wrong. Shaking the hitbox during hit stop, letting damage percentage change knockback on the early hits of a multi-hit move, or letting a stance change slide the target back all make hits that should connect miss.
how_to_apply: Make collision wider than the visible weapon in fast games and make sure each attack's range crosses the median line where opponents stand. During hit stop, shake only the rendered model. Give every hit but the last of a multi-hit move fixed knockback. Test strings against every reaction stance so the target's top node doesn't drift. When a hit feels off, adjust the hitbox and the animation together. Check reach in every direction and in ground and aerial versions.
anti_pattern: Pixel-exact hitboxes in a fast game; hitboxes that shake with the model; fixing a misplaced animation by stretching collision to meet it; assuming a combo works because it works at one damage level.
example: Smash Bros. attack collision is wider than the fighter's sword or fist. Mario's Super Jump Punch uses fixed knockback on its early hits. A neutral-attack combo missed because the hit fighter's top node moved back. Pyra's forward aerial collision was shortened because it kept hitting after the swing; Steve's grab arc was pulled closer; Sora's Sonic Blade lost reach when aimed upward.
review_question: Does every attack that visibly connects register, at every damage level and from every direction, and does anything keep hitting after the swing has visibly ended?
keywords: hitbox hurtbox collision attack range whiff missed hits fairness multi-hit combos connect hit detection generous hitboxes median line top node

principle: Keep every wait and transition hasty, but don't cut it out entirely
why: Making players wait is a sin. Slow fades followed by long black screens leave players without control and rob them of their time, and it is almost impossible to make a transition too fast. Removing transitions altogether feels jarring, though. Some load times can't be optimized away; what really irritates is a wait that looks like someone dropped the ball.
how_to_apply: Time every fade, black screen and non-interactive stretch, then trim each one to 'a hasty speed' that still reads as a transition. Hide unavoidable loading inside an in-world moment or a themed wipe; if you can't, show a simple, world-styled loading indicator straight away. Don't time presentation to development-build load times, which will change. Let any press during a cutscene bring up a skip, and let cutscenes pause.
anti_pattern: Slow, dreary fades and long black screens; hard cuts with no transition; a loading icon on top of a transition that is already hiding the load; presentation whose length depends on today's load times.
example: The original Resident Evil's doors hid loading, built fear and opened a little slower when zombies waited behind them. The first Legend of Zelda scrolls at screen edges so players see how the map connects (today it could be smoother and faster). Super Mario World's key transition adds mystery; Smash Ultimate uses random wipes into the victory screen.
review_question: How many seconds of a typical session is the player not in control, and does any wait look like a development mistake?
keywords: screen transitions fades wipes loading screens load times waiting player time black screen skip cutscenes pause downtime speed

principle: Make failure hit hard for about a second, then hand back control
why: Player interest cools fast between 'Ugh, I blew it!' and getting control back, and the longer the wait the more they lose interest. Quick retries raise their tolerance for difficulty. The loss should still really be felt, so the failure effect must be flashy and impactful, but short. The game moving on its own isn't enough; the player has to be in control.
how_to_apply: Measure the time from failure to control. Keep the failure effect flashy and to 'a second or so' (genre-dependent), then return control as soon as possible. Trim loads and non-interactive screens; if a step must remain, make it player-advanced. Don't respawn players into enemy fire. Keep some real cost so respawning never feels mindless.
anti_pattern: Long death animations, slow fades and loading between failure and retry; infinite respawns right where the player died; players losing again before they touch the controller.
example: No specific game is cited in the retry episode. In Kirby's Adventure the action stops when Kirby loses a life, and Fantasy Zone's hit stop gives an 'oh no!' moment, both short and clear.
review_question: How long from the moment of failure until the player can act again, and is the failure itself unmistakable?
keywords: retry restart death respawn failure effect game over quick retry player time loss feedback checkpoint frustration

principle: Specify, feel and verify every timing in frames
why: Games measure time in frames, and distance = time x speed, so frames are the basis for all movement. There is no stopwatch for frames, so a designer must train a sense of them to write precise specs and to notice when code or data errors make the build differ from the spec.
how_to_apply: Assume a target rate (at 60 fps, 60 frames is one second). Train by clapping '1-and-2-and-3-and': about 30 frames per beat, 15 per half beat. Anchor on known moves (about 15 frames from Smash Attack input to release, about 15 for a standard Tekken kick's startup, a bit under half that for a Street Fighter II heavy punch) and estimate from the 0/15/30 anchors. Write specs as frame numbers (attack start frame, total frames) and speeds per frame. Lock processing speed and frame timing before final tuning.
anti_pattern: Words like 'quick' or 'slow' in specs; frame counts nobody on the team can feel or verify; tuning balance while frame timing is still changing.
example: His NES and SNES games counted time in screen interrupts, so the 50 fps PAL versions ran at 5/6 speed. Meteos became harder than intended when processing speed changed late in development.
review_question: Is every timing in the spec a frame number, and could its author tell by feel whether the build matches?
keywords: frames frame counting frame data timing unit of time 60 fps startup frames specs spec sheet durations distance time speed 1-and-2-and

principle: Sell hit stop with shake, scaling and blending, not a bare freeze
why: A plain stop works, but in Smash hit stop is never just a stop; there is always some shake. Each technique is hard to notice on its own, but together they make hits feel much stronger. Scaling by strength plus a multiplier lets a sweet spot feel heavier than its damage and lets guest characters feel like their source games.
how_to_apply: Shake the victim more and the attacker less, moving only the rendered model. Shake grounded characters horizontally only and airborne ones in all directions, starting big and decaying over the precomputed stop length. Compute stop length from attack strength, then apply a per-move multiplier; lengthen it for lightning and shorten it in multiplayer. Increase shake when the camera is pulled back. Blend the victim into the damage pose over about four frames. Keep a sword attacker's animation creeping forward very slowly (per-attack toggle). Let hit marks keep animating and let the hit sound's main body finish during the stop.
anti_pattern: Shaking the hitbox; vertical shake on grounded 3D characters, which clips legs into the floor; one fixed stop length for every hit; a frozen victim snapped to a single pose.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the tip of Marth's sword gets a bigger stop than its base; Ryu's stops look bigger and Kazuya's smaller at equal damage to match their games; a strong sword swing's tip keeps inching upward during the stop. Final Fight's hit stop left a lasting impression.
review_question: During hit stop, does the victim shake more than the attacker, does duration scale with strength, and does anything still move or animate?
keywords: hitstop hit stop shake hit shake freeze impact multiplier sweet spot victim attacker hitbox damage pose blend hit lag hit pause

principle: Front-load the hit and make strong attacks pay for it in recovery
why: Lead-ins should move quickly into the attack for responsiveness, but if you want push and pull, strong attacks must leave the character proportionally vulnerable afterward or the game feels unrefined. Landing a slow, risky move is a more commendable feat, so it earns more damage and knockback. Recovery length is also a balance lever that can change a move without touching its signature power.
how_to_apply: Lay out each attack so the hit registers about 1/4 to 1/3 of the way in (about 1/5 for fast moves), with standard attacks finishing in under a second. Scale recovery with power; even Smash Attacks with large openings almost never exceed one second. When a move is too strong, lengthen its follow-through or shrink its hitbox rather than cutting what defines it.
anti_pattern: Strong attacks with little vulnerability afterward; slow windups that delay responsiveness instead of long recoveries that create openings; nerfing a move's identity when its recovery could change instead.
example: Super Smash Bros.: the quick, safe neutral attack against the slow, vulnerable Smash Attack that earns more damage and knockback; attack breakdowns marking hit, end and cancel points.
review_question: For every attack, where does the hit land in its timeline, and does a stronger move leave the attacker open for longer?
keywords: recovery end lag vulnerability startup active frames frame data attack timeline risk reward push and pull punish window move balance

principle: Return control when players expect it, using cancel frames
why: Cancel frames let players move, jump or attack again before the animation fully returns to standby, a bit of elbow room. Smash didn't have them until after Melee, so control only came back at standby, which felt a little heavy or rigid. Their timing has to match when people instinctively expect control back.
how_to_apply: Mark a cancel window in the latter part of each recovery. When an input arrives during it, blend from the current pose into the new action. Playtest whether the window lines up with when players try to act, and keep the recovery pose visibly held up to that point.
anti_pattern: Returning control only after the full return to standby; cancel windows so early that recovery stops meaning anything; snapping into the next animation instead of blending.
example: Super Smash Bros. through Melee had no cancel frames and felt a little rigid; later games mark where cancel frames end the recovery.
review_question: Do players regain control at the moment they instinctively try to act after each move?
keywords: cancel frames animation cancel interrupt recovery control return elbow room IASA rigid controls heavy controls blend into next action

principle: Shape the jump's rise, fall and air control to your game's goal
why: A jump is simple but full of choices, and the right one depends on what the game is for. Even with the same trajectory, changing a move's speed drastically changes how it feels. A gentle rise and fast fall suit variable-height platforming, a floaty jump helps when the height you shoot from matters, and a fixed arc turns every jump into a planned commitment.
how_to_apply: Build the jump from an initial upward velocity plus downward acceleration added every frame, with a maximum fall speed. Use separate rise and fall gravity. Decide air control on purpose. For slams, make the descent faster than the ascent. If jump and up-attacks share an input, keep a short, uniform pre-jump windup. For forgiving escapes, use a very strong burst then heavy gravity for a few frames before normal gravity. Ask each project whether you need a jump at all.
anti_pattern: One default jump reused across games; removing the pre-jump windup when up-attacks share the stick direction; a camera that hides jump height.
example: Super Mario Bros. (gentle rise, sudden extra gravity at the peak, hold for height); Metroid (slow rise, slow fall); Ghosts 'n Goblins (low jump, no mid-air steering); Zangief's Spinning Pile Driver falls faster than it rises from Street Fighter II Turbo on; Smash Ultimate and Kirby Super Star's burst jump.
review_question: Can you state what your jump's rise, peak, fall and air control are each for?
keywords: jump physics gravity jump arc rise fall speed air control variable jump height fall speed apex jump windup jump squat platforming

principle: Sell big impacts with screen shake tuned to the camera
why: Screen shake is just the ticket for conveying a big impact; a game without it can feel bland and even a tiny shake changes how hard attacks feel. But too much makes the screen hard to see, and in 3D a camera shake barely moves distant objects, so the amount needs real care.
how_to_apply: Author a few distinct presets (Smash uses large, medium, small, extra-small) with different axis behavior, not scaled copies. Start strong and decay with a little randomness. Shake the camera's look-at point as much as the camera or more. Scale amplitude by camera distance and field of view, and retune scenes with unusual FOV. Reserve it for impacts that deserve it, and pair it with a brief full-screen flash only for the heaviest ones.
anti_pattern: Shaking until the screen is unreadable; moving a distant look-at point so subtly nothing seems to happen; one shake scaled up and down for every impact; shipping big impacts with no shake.
example: Super Smash Bros.: small shakes vertical only, medium adds horizontal, large shakes more; Flat Zone's tight field of view made normal shake feel too big, so it was retuned. Sakurai has used shake often since Kirby's Adventure.
review_question: Does each impact class have its own shake, and does the shake look the same size at every camera distance?
keywords: screen shake camera shake shake presets trauma impact rumble field of view camera distance decay randomness screen flash

principle: Tune on-screen response so each character has its own weight
why: The same physical button can feel light or heavy depending on movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag and frame rate: somehow you feel feedback with your hands. Control feel can be the fun by itself, like an RC car. Differences in speed, vulnerability and animation flair create push and pull and characters that feel wildly different. Inertia is also a risk dial: more of it raises game essence but narrows appeal.
how_to_apply: Decide each character's intended weight, then tune speed, inertia and jump physics to it and compare characters with identical inputs. Run them on one shared behavior and express differences as parameter sets. Reserve schedule time just to sense and fine-tune movement. Set analog tilt sensitivity per console.
anti_pattern: Assuming feel comes from hardware; characters that differ only in stats you can't feel; adding inertia without considering who it shuts out.
example: NES control-pad games that feel radically different; Family BASIC's SPRITE command, a controller-driven sprite with a little inertia, taught Sakurai lessons he used on Kirby's Dream Land; every Kirby Air Ride machine shares one behavior and differs by parameters; a hypothetical harder Kirby with more inertia.
review_question: With the same inputs, does each character feel like the weight you intended, and does moving feel good on its own?
keywords: game feel weight heavy light inertia acceleration movement speed control feel character feel button weight parameters momentum

principle: Frame the camera for the gameplay, not just to follow the character
why: With the camera's center point anchored to the character, it's hard to see how the character is moving: jump height disappears and dodges lose impact. Good framing improves presentation, and the right frame differs by game: look-ahead for side-scrollers, an anchored point only where precise realistic racing suits it.
how_to_apply: Track the center point less (or not at all) on the Y axis during jumps. Let the character drift off center during dodges and drifts. In side-scrollers show more space ahead. In co-op scrollers make one player the camera's lead and warp stragglers back. When a character is knocked flying, stop scrolling, then gently recenter once they settle. Treat camera inertia as a tunable value.
anti_pattern: Anchoring the center point to the character by default; full vertical tracking that hides jumps; giving every co-op player equal pull on the scroll.
example: Super Mario 64 (Mario rises on screen when he jumps) against Smash Ultimate with a fighter-tracking camera; Armored Core; Kirby Air Ride drifting; Kirby Super Star's Helper system and Space Jump; Kirby's Dream Land's 1990 design document; Kid Icarus: Uprising's swipe-to-spin touch aiming.
review_question: When the character jumps, dodges or gets launched, can the player see on screen how far they moved?
keywords: camera center point look-at point camera tracking framing look-ahead co-op camera off-center vertical tracking camera inertia knockback camera

principle: Keep controls simple and physical, and no busier than the game needs
why: By 1996 fighting-game command inputs had become extremely complicated, so Smash used a stick direction plus a button, which players pick up intuitively. Reading how far and how fast the analog stick moves gives the controls real physicality. One button can already carry a whole game, and each added input changes how it feels; the simplest approach often plays best.
how_to_apply: Map moves to direction plus button and use input timing (a quick flick) for stronger variants. Scale walk speed by tilt and trigger dashes with a fast flick instead of a double-tap or held button. Try the core action on one button before adding more. Make the dominant action's button the most prominent only when actions are unequal. On new hardware, list what the device uniquely does and adopt only the uses that fit. Lower input density for casual audiences or laggy online play.
anti_pattern: Long command strings; two-step or two-button basic actions; adding inputs because the hardware has them; rapid tapping as a core mechanic; high input density for a casual audience.
example: Smash's smash input and flick input ('Tap' in the N64 version); Kid Icarus: Uprising's flick dash and dodge and its context-sensitive attack button; Brawl not using every Nunchuk or pointer function; Kirby's one-button minigames; the GameCube controller's big A button.
review_question: Could a newcomer perform every core action within minutes, and does each input earn its place?
keywords: controls simple controls input design one button analog stick flick input tilt dash input density control scheme peripherals intuitive

principle: Never let a deliberate input feel canceled or misread
why: If a small forward nudge from an action drops the player off a ledge, it feels like their input was canceled. If jumps start instantly, players jump before they can input an up-attack on the same stick direction. Flick dashes have accidental dashes as a downside. Ambiguous responses leave players unsure what happened. Each of these breaks trust in the controls.
how_to_apply: Decide ledge behavior per action: keep short stepping attacks and forward dodges on the platform, let fast rushes carry over, stop long rushes late in the move, and use speed thresholds for rolling moves. For walking, consider requiring a push toward the edge or steering along near-parallel ledges. Keep a short, uniform windup where two inputs share a direction. Expose flick sensitivity as a setting. Playtest ledges and edge cases by feel.
anti_pattern: Characters that fall off every ledge unconditionally; ignoring momentum so it's easy to fly off the stage; inputs that silently do something other than what was meant.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Fox Illusion stops at the ledge; Falcon Kick goes over unless the ledge is reached late in the move; Drill Rush stops at the ledge late; Egg Roll uses a speed parameter; the unified jump windup protects Up Smash; Ultimate's flick sensitivity option.
review_question: Is there any situation where the player pressed one thing and the game did something else, like walking off a ledge or dashing by accident?
keywords: ledges edge behavior input intent canceled input accidental input ledge falling momentum jump windup flick sensitivity misread input forgiveness

principle: Build knockback as a tunable payoff with per-attack parameters
why: When launching opponents is the core mechanic, knockback is at the heart of the game essence and needs unorthodox detail to feel fun. A launcher should cause at least some reaction on a barely damaged opponent, multi-hit moves must connect at any damage level, and big launches after a struggle give a visceral thrill. Launches also have to stay readable on small screens.
how_to_apply: Compute knockback from attack damage and the target's accumulated damage. Give each attack a free launch angle, an optional modifier toward the attacker's direction of travel, a multiplier, a guaranteed minimum kept in check by scaling, and an optional fixed value. Let target weight and fall speed shape the arc. Cap launch speed for readability on the smallest target screen.
anti_pattern: Adding a minimum knockback without scaling, which makes launches too big; damage-dependent knockback on early hits of a multi-hit move; launches too fast to follow on a handheld screen.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Mario's Super Jump Punch (fixed knockback until the final hit); launch speed slowed in Smash for 3DS to stay readable on its LCD; Ultimate sped knockback up again. Kirby's Dream Land's 1990 design document already tied knockback distance to health.
review_question: Does every attack produce a visible, intended reaction at low, medium and high damage, and can players follow the launch?
keywords: knockback launch angle knockback scaling base knockback fixed knockback multiplier weight fall speed combos launcher hitstun

principle: Choose your frame rate on purpose and protect it
why: 60 fps and 30 fps differ in look and in how smoothly they control. 60 fps is ideal; 30 fps is a common, more than adequate standard, because drawing twice the frames costs half your visual performance. For Smash on 3DS Sakurai treated a stable 60 fps as an absolute must and cut content until it held. A port that keeps every element but drops frames loses its smoothness and mood.
how_to_apply: Pick the target rate early by weighing control smoothness against the rendering budget. If the game is timing-heavy, hold a stable 60 and pare content and effects rather than dropping to 30. Keep game speed independent of how many frames are drawn; a variable frame rate is not slowdown. Check high refresh rates against displays that can show them.
anti_pattern: Deciding the frame rate late; confusing frame drops with slowdown; tying game logic to a refresh rate that varies by region or platform.
example: Smash for 3DS kept four players, stereoscopic 3D and items at a stable 60 fps; the NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept everything in place but lost its smoothness and creepiness; Smash Ultimate's stages were built for eight fighters at 60 fps.
review_question: Does the game hold its target frame rate in the worst case, and was that target chosen for the controls rather than by default?
keywords: frame rate fps 60 fps 30 fps performance budget stable frame rate slowdown variable frame rate smoothness refresh rate

principle: Use genre-standard controls, keep series rules stable, and allow remapping
why: De facto standards let you skip explanations and warm the handshake between human and computer. Changing a series' basic rules and controls with every release makes it harder to play. Designers once assumed their layout was best and nobody would change it, but players want the freedom to play their way.
how_to_apply: Map core actions to the genre's standard buttons unless you have a deliberate reason not to. Keep rotation rules, previews and similar fundamentals identical across a series. Ship a remapping screen: a drawn controller, pick the button with the cursor then the action, let several buttons share an action, and save named profiles. Expose stick and flick sensitivity. Remap awkward legacy schemes when re-releasing old games.
anti_pattern: Avoiding standards so you don't look like a copy; reinventing basic rules each sequel; fixed controls on modern controllers.
example: Western FPS games share nearly the same controls; old Tetris versions each felt different until the 2002 guidelines; Pac-Land's run-by-pressing scheme became easy after remapping in Arcade Archives; Smash's two jump buttons and named profiles.
review_question: Would a player of this genre know the controls without being told, and can every player change them?
keywords: standard controls conventions button remapping key config control profiles sensitivity settings de facto standards series consistency

principle: Retune every feel parameter when tempo, mode or hardware changes
why: Raising Smash Ultimate's tempo meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused, jumps and knockback included. Fighters dropped into Brawl's Subspace Emissary with their versus specs didn't work. Different hardware changes what reads well, and a late change in processing speed can silently break tuning.
how_to_apply: When the game's speed changes, budget time to rebuild movement and combat values rather than porting them. Give characters a separate movement parameter set for very different modes. Let the weakest target screen set shared speed limits. Redo tuning if performance changes late.
anti_pattern: Carrying old tuning into a faster or slower game; one parameter set for incompatible modes; reusing raw speed values across platforms with different pixel counts.
example: Ultimate's tempo sits between Melee and Smash for; Brawl was slowed for casual players; Smash for 3DS slowed launches for its LCD; Meteos became harder after a late processing-speed change; PAL ports ran at 5/6 speed.
review_question: Since the last change in tempo, mode or platform, has every movement and combat value been re-felt, not just carried over?
keywords: tempo game speed retuning parameters sequels porting modes parameter sets platform differences balance retune

principle: State speeds in shared units and judge them against body size
why: Speed = distance / time, and specs don't work if the team can't share what a speed means. Pixel counts differ between platforms, so the same value gives different results. A speed that looks low in km/h can be fast for a tiny character.
how_to_apply: Pick one unit per project (pixels per frame for sprites; km/h or distance per frame for real-scale 3D), document it and put it in parameter names. Build at real-world scale if you want real speeds. Judge speeds against the character's own size. Practice estimating speeds by eye before checking the number.
anti_pattern: Speeds without units; reusing raw speed values across resolutions; judging speed only by the number.
example: Mario's top speed in Mario Bros. is about 1 p/f on a 256-pixel-wide NES screen (Sakurai's guess); Kirby Air Ride used km/h, which look low because Kirby is about a 20 cm square.
review_question: Does every speed in your specs have a unit everyone reads the same way?
keywords: speed units pixels per frame p/f km/h distance per frame scale movement speed specs parameters

principle: Treat the screen as a small window and spend it on play
why: A screen covers only about 30 degrees of the player's vision, so a wide world is squeezed into a narrow window and screen space is scarce. Realistic views like a cockpit camera shrink the space left for play, and tiny distant targets lack impact.
how_to_apply: Before choosing camera and field of view, decide what must fit on screen. Prefer views that leave more room for play. If targets look tiny, scale them up. Weigh VR's blur and head-turning costs, and favor it where gaze and heading differ.
anti_pattern: Choosing a view for realism at the cost of play space; tiny targets on a big screen.
example: Racing games mostly avoid the cockpit view; Kid Icarus: Uprising made standard enemies four or five times Pit's size; VR racing suits games where you look somewhere other than where you move.
review_question: How much of the screen is actually used for play in your main camera, and are targets big enough to read?
keywords: screen space field of view FOV camera view cockpit view target size VR screen real estate

principle: Offer comfort toggles instead of stripping presentation for everyone
why: 3D motion sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear doesn't feel. Turning off footstep shake can help a lot, but a camera built to avoid sickness has little embellishment and looks less entertaining. Too much shake or blur also makes the action hard to read.
how_to_apply: List inertia-heavy camera effects (footstep bob, vehicle-frame sway, blur) and give each an option. Lock cockpit or vehicle frames in place in a comfort mode. Offer a blur-strength setting. Cap shake and flash so the screen stays readable. Recruit testers who actually get sick.
anti_pattern: Assuming the camera is comfortable because nobody on the team gets sick; removing presentation for everyone instead of offering options.
example: The common FPS option to disable vertical footstep shake; games that let players adjust motion blur.
review_question: Can a player prone to motion sickness turn off every inertial camera effect without losing the game's readability?
keywords: motion sickness comfort options accessibility head bob camera shake toggle motion blur setting vehicle sway

principle: Tune feel by hand, with exposed parameters and fast iteration
why: Sakurai learned how changes affect feel by tinkering with sprite inertia in Family BASIC. Feel is found by trying values and playing, and tuning is where you iterate most, so values must be easy to change and the build easy to test. Ledge behavior and similar details only show up by paying attention to feel in playtesting.
how_to_apply: Keep every speed, timing and force in parameters outside the code, name them in plain language with units, and push edits to builds in one step. Build debug commands for the setups you test most (set damage percentage, slow motion, hide background). Vary one value at a time and note how it feels.
anti_pattern: Hard-coded values that need a programmer for every tweak; tuning by spreadsheet without playing; slow conversion loops.
example: Family BASIC's SPRITE command; Smash parameters in Excel with one-button conversion; '[Special X-deceleration is O/frame]' bracket notation; Kirby Air Ride machines tuned by a few numbers; the Training Mode trajectory guide began as a debug feature.
review_question: How long does it take to change one movement value and feel the result in the build?
keywords: tuning iteration parameters prototyping debug tools game feel tuning inertia experiment playtesting feel parameter spreadsheet
